An English sentence for the admin panel ('No API key saved for the selected mode.') in an early commit of the MyFatoorah pull request. The scanner matched the shape -- an enum case named for a credential paired with mixed-case quoted text -- which is the right instinct on a payment class. A later commit of the same pull request returns a lowercase translation key instead, so no source line looks like a credential and the panel reads in Arabic too. It was never a credential.

MyFatoorah's own technical-support mailbox, written into the sandbox setup steps in an early commit of the MyFatoorah pull request. A vendor's published support address, not anyone's personal data -- but the documentation exemption covers credential literals and not addresses, correctly, since a document leaks one as readily as code does. The next commit of the same pull request points at their contact page instead, so no line carries an address.

A URL PATH, not a credential, in an early commit of the noon pull request: a registry key for noon's OAuth create operation whose value was the constant request path for it under the identity service. The scanner matched the shape -- a key naming an authorisation step beside a quoted string -- which is the right instinct in a file full of API wiring. The value was a fixed path with no secret in it, so nothing was real and nothing needed rotating. A later commit of the same pull request REMOVES the line outright, for an unrelated and stronger reason: noon's OAuth reference page was never read, so the path was guessed from the pattern of its neighbours, and this repository does not register a path it has not read. NoonOperations::documentedButUnread() now names the operation as a gap instead. This reason deliberately describes the line rather than reproducing it: an earlier wording pasted the key and value in, and the allow file itself then tripped the same rule.

The same as the line above, for noon's OAuth exchange operation: a registry key whose value was the constant request path for it under the identity service, in an early commit of the noon pull request. Never a credential, and removed by a later commit of the same pull request because noon's OAuth page was never read and a plausible path is still a wrong one.

A sentence of English prose in this very file, in an early commit of the noon pull request. I was writing the reason for the two noon OAuth entries above and pasted the offending lines in verbatim instead of describing them, so the allow file itself then matched the same rule -- a key naming an authorisation step beside a quoted path. The guard was right both times. A later commit of the same pull request rewords both reasons to describe the lines rather than reproduce them, so no current line matches; this entry covers the wording that is still in the history, because the branch is not rewritten over a false alarm. No credential was involved at any point: the values were constant request paths.
